tool.name: Ruby
tool.tagline: Expressive, object-oriented language designed for programmer happiness
tool.description: Ruby is a dynamic, fully object-oriented language with a clean syntax built around blocks and message passing. It powers Ruby on Rails and tools like Homebrew, Jekyll and Chef, and is loved for scripting and DSLs. Learning Ruby teaches you a flexible object model and an idiomatic, collection-oriented style that carries over to many languages.

concepts.name: Running Ruby
concepts.summary: Run Ruby scripts and IRB, print with puts and p, and meet Ruby's everything-is-an-object idea.
concepts.why: Every Ruby journey starts with running code and inspecting values, and IRB is where Rubyists experiment.
concepts.body:
Ruby code lives in `.rb` files and runs with `ruby hello.rb`. For experiments, start **IRB**, the interactive Ruby shell, with `irb`: type an expression and it prints the result. `ruby -e 'puts 1 + 1'` runs a one-liner, and `ruby -v` shows the version.

Three ways to print:

- `puts x` prints `x.to_s` followed by a newline (arrays print one element per line).
- `print x` prints without a newline.
- `p x` prints `x.inspect`, the developer view: strings keep their quotes, and `nil` is shown as `nil`. It also returns its argument, so you can wrap it around an expression while debugging.

In Ruby **everything is an object**, including numbers, `nil` and `true`. You call methods on them with a dot: `5.even?`, `"ruby".upcase`, `nil.to_a`. Even `1 + 2` is the method call `1.+(2)`.

Comments start with `#`. Parentheses around method arguments are optional (`puts "hi"` and `puts("hi")` are the same), and statements end at the line break, without semicolons.

By convention, methods ending in `?` return a boolean (`empty?`), and methods ending in `!` are the "dangerous" version of a method, usually one that modifies the receiver in place (`upcase!`).
concepts.code:
# hello.rb: run with `ruby hello.rb`
puts "Hello, Ruby!"        # Hello, Ruby!
puts RUBY_VERSION          # e.g. 3.4.7

p "quoted"                 # "quoted"
puts nil.inspect           # nil

puts 5.even?               # false
puts "ruby".upcase         # RUBY
puts 1.+(2)                # 3: operators are methods
puts 42.class              # Integer
puts nil.class             # NilClass
takeaways: Run files with ruby file.rb and experiment in irb
puts shows to_s, p shows inspect (great for debugging)
Everything is an object; operators are method calls
pitfalls: Using puts to debug and missing that a value is nil or a string; use p instead.

quiz.q: What does p "hi" print?
quiz.explain: p prints the inspect form, which keeps the quotes around strings.

concepts.name: Variables, numbers and nil
concepts.summary: Assign variables and work with Integer, Float, String, Symbol, true, false and nil, including Ruby's truthiness rule.
concepts.why: Ruby's simple truthiness rule and its numeric types shape how every condition and calculation behaves.
concepts.body:
Local variables need no declaration: `count = 3`. Names are `snake_case`. Constants start with a capital letter, `MAX_SIZE = 10`, and Ruby warns if you reassign one.

Core value types:

- **Integer** has arbitrary precision: `2**100` just works. Integer division truncates toward negative infinity: `7 / 2` is `3` and `-7 / 2` is `-4`. Use `7.fdiv(2)` or a float operand for `3.5`.
- **Float** is a double: `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`. Use `Rational` or `BigDecimal` for money.
- **String** is mutable text, and **Symbol** (`:name`) is an immutable, interned name, mostly used as hash keys and identifiers.
- `true`, `false` and `nil` ("no value").

The truthiness rule is simple: **only `false` and `nil` are falsy**. `0`, `""` and `[]` are all truthy, unlike in many languages. Check for nothing with `x.nil?` and for emptiness with `empty?`.

Conversions are explicit: `"42".to_i`, `"3.5".to_f`, `42.to_s`, `:sym.to_s`, `"str".to_sym`. The lenient `"12abc".to_i` returns `12`; the strict `Integer("12abc")` raises `ArgumentError`, which is what you want for validating input.

`x ||= 5` assigns only if `x` is nil or false, a common idiom for defaults and memoisation. Safe navigation `user&.name` returns nil instead of raising when `user` is nil.
concepts.code:
count = 3
price = 9.5
big = 2**100
puts big                 # 1267650600228229401496703205376
puts 7 / 2, -7 / 2       # 3, -4
puts 7.fdiv(2)           # 3.5
puts 0.1 + 0.2           # 0.30000000000000004

puts "zero is truthy" if 0     # zero is truthy
puts [nil, false, 0, ""].map { |v| v ? "T" : "F" }.join  # FFTT

puts "12abc".to_i        # 12
begin
  Integer("12abc")
rescue ArgumentError
  puts "strict parse failed"   # strict parse failed
end

name = nil
name ||= "guest"
p name                   # "guest"
p nil&.length            # nil
takeaways: Only false and nil are falsy; 0 and "" are truthy
Integers are arbitrary precision and / on integers truncates
Use Integer() and Float() for strict parsing, to_i for lenient
pitfalls: Writing if count.zero? style checks as if count, which is always true for numbers.

quiz.q: Which of these values is falsy in Ruby?
quiz.explain: Only nil and false are falsy; every other value, including 0 and empty strings, is truthy.

quiz.q: What is -7 / 2 in Ruby?
quiz.explain: Integer division rounds toward negative infinity, so -3.5 becomes -4.

concepts.name: Conditionals, loops and case
concepts.summary: Branch with if, unless and case/when, use modifier forms, and loop with while, until and times.
concepts.why: Ruby's conditionals are expressions, and its idioms (modifiers, unless, case with ranges) read almost like English.
concepts.body:
`if`/`elsif`/`else`/`end` and `unless` (the negation of `if`) work as expected. In Ruby these are **expressions**: they return the value of the branch taken, so `label = if score > 50 then "pass" else "fail" end` is valid. The ternary `cond ? a : b` covers short cases.

**Modifier forms** put the condition after a single statement: `return if list.empty?`, `retry_later unless connected?`. They are idiomatic for guard clauses. Avoid `unless` with `else` or with negations; it gets hard to read.

`case`/`when` compares using `===`, the "case equality" operator, so a `when` can be a value, a class, a range or a regex:

```ruby
case input
when Integer then "number"
when 1..5 then "small"     # Range#=== checks inclusion
when /\A\d+\z/ then "digits" # Regexp#=== matches
else "other"
end
```

Loops: `while cond ... end`, `until cond ... end` and `loop do ... end` (exit with `break`). In practice Rubyists rarely write `for`; they use iterators: `3.times { |i| ... }`, `1.upto(5)`, `array.each`. Inside blocks and loops, `next` skips to the next iteration and `break` exits.

`&&`, `||` and `!` are the logical operators. The words `and`, `or` and `not` exist but have very low precedence; use them only for control flow like `save or raise "failed"`, never in conditions.
concepts.code:
def classify(x)
  case x
  when Integer then x.negative? ? "negative" : "integer"
  when 0.0..1.0 then "fraction"
  when /\A\w+@\w+\.\w+\z/ then "email"
  when nil then "missing"
  else "unknown"
  end
end

[5, -2, 0.5, "a@b.io", nil, :x].each { |v| puts classify(v) }
# integer negative fraction email missing unknown (one per line)

grade = if 72 >= 70 then "pass" else "fail" end
puts grade                   # pass

3.times { |i| print i, " " } # 0 1 2
puts
n = 0
n += 1 until n * n > 50
puts n                       # 8
takeaways: if, unless and case are expressions that return a value
case/when uses ===, so classes, ranges and regexes all work
Prefer iterators like times and each over for loops
pitfalls: Using and/or in assignments: x = true and false sets x to true because = binds tighter.

quiz.q: Why does when Integer match 5 in a case statement?
options: Integer === 5 is true because Class#=== checks instance membership
case converts both sides to strings
quiz.explain: case/when calls pattern === value, and Class#=== tests whether the value is an instance of the class.

concepts.name: Strings and symbols
concepts.summary: Interpolate and manipulate strings, understand mutability and frozen literals, and know when to use symbols.
concepts.why: Text processing is everywhere, and Ruby's string API plus symbols are used in every Ruby program.
concepts.body:
Double-quoted strings interpolate with `#{}` and process escapes: `"Hi #{name}\n"`. Single-quoted strings are literal. Heredocs build multi-line text, and the squiggly form `<<~TEXT` strips the common leading indentation.

The String API is large and readable: `upcase`, `capitalize`, `strip`, `split`, `include?`, `start_with?`, `sub`/`gsub` (with strings or regexes), `center`, `ljust`, `*` for repetition, and `[]` with an index, range or regex. `format("%.2f", x)` and `"%05d" % n` format numbers.

Ruby strings are **mutable**. `<<` appends in place, and bang methods like `upcase!` modify the receiver (returning nil if nothing changed). Non-bang methods return a new string. Two variables can share one string object, so in-place changes are visible through both.

Adding `# frozen_string_literal: true` at the top of a file makes all literals frozen (immutable). In Ruby 3.4, literals in files without the comment are "chilled": mutating them still works but emits a deprecation warning when deprecation warnings are enabled, as a step toward frozen literals by default. Use `+""` or `String.new` when you need a mutable buffer.

A **Symbol** like `:status` is an immutable name; the same symbol is always the same object. Use symbols for identifiers and hash keys, strings for text data. `str.to_sym` and `sym.to_s` convert between them.
concepts.code:
# frozen_string_literal: true
name = "Ruby"
puts "Hi #{name}, #{name.length} chars"   # Hi Ruby, 4 chars
puts 'No #{interp} here'                  # No #{interp} here

text = <<~MSG
  Dear #{name},
    indented line
MSG
puts text                                 # leading indentation removed

puts "a,b,,c".split(",").inspect          # ["a", "b", "", "c"]
puts "hello world".gsub(/o/, "0")         # hell0 w0rld
puts format("%.2f|%5s|", 3.14159, "x")    # 3.14|    x|

buf = +""            # mutable even with frozen literals
buf << "a" << "b"
puts buf             # ab
puts "lit".frozen?   # true (magic comment)
puts :ok.equal?(:ok) # true: one object per symbol
takeaways: Use "#{}" for interpolation and <<~ for indented heredocs
Bang methods and << mutate; most other methods return new strings
Symbols are immutable identifiers; strings are text data
pitfalls: Modifying a string that another variable also references, then being surprised both changed.

quiz.q: With # frozen_string_literal: true, what happens on s = "abc"; s << "d"?
options: A new string is silently created
quiz.explain: The literal is frozen, so mutating it raises FrozenError; use +"abc" or dup for a mutable copy.

concepts.name: Arrays, hashes and ranges
concepts.summary: Create and access arrays, hashes and ranges, including default values and symbol-key shorthand.
concepts.why: Nearly all Ruby data, from JSON to Rails params, is handled as arrays and hashes.
concepts.body:
An **Array** is an ordered, growable list of any objects: `nums = [3, 1, 2]`. Index from the front or back (`nums[0]`, `nums[-1]`), slice with `nums[0, 2]` or `nums[1..]`, and add with `push`/`<<`, `unshift`, `pop`, `shift`. Out-of-range reads return `nil`; `fetch(i)` raises instead. `%w[a b c]` builds an array of strings.

A **Hash** maps keys to values and keeps insertion order. With symbol keys, use the shorthand `{ name: "Ada", age: 36 }`; other keys use `=>`: `{ "id" => 1 }`. Note that `:name` and `"name"` are different keys, a common source of nil surprises with parsed JSON.

- `h[:missing]` returns `nil` (or the hash's default); `h.fetch(:k)` raises `KeyError`, and `h.fetch(:k, 0)` gives a fallback.
- `Hash.new(0)` makes missing keys read as 0, perfect for counters. For mutable defaults use the block form `Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = [] }`.
- `key?`, `keys`, `values`, `delete`, `merge`, `dig(:a, :b)` and `to_a` are everyday tools.

**Ranges** like `1..5` (inclusive) and `1...5` (exclusive end) represent intervals; endless `1..` and beginless `..10` work too. Convert with `to_a`, test membership with `include?` or `cover?`.

Destructure arrays with `first, *rest = list`. Since Ruby 3.1 you can omit a hash value when a local variable has the same name: `{ name:, age: }`.
takeaways: Symbol keys and string keys are different
Use fetch when a missing key is a bug; Hash.new(0) for counters
Ranges: .. includes the end, ... excludes it
pitfalls: Using Hash.new([]) for grouping: every key shares the same array object. Use the block form.

quiz.q: What does Hash.new([]) cause when you do h[:a] << 1; h[:b] << 2?
options: h is still empty and the shared default array is [1, 2]
quiz.explain: << mutates the single default array without storing any key; use Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = [] }.

concepts.name: Defining methods
concepts.summary: Define methods with positional, optional, keyword and splat arguments, and rely on implicit returns.
concepts.why: Methods are the unit of reuse in Ruby, and keyword arguments are the idiomatic way to keep call sites readable.
concepts.body:
Define a method with `def name(params) ... end`. The value of the **last expression** is returned automatically; `return` is only needed to exit early. Endless methods (Ruby 3.0) fit one-liners: `def square(x) = x * x`.

Parameter kinds, in the order they must appear:

- Required positional: `def greet(name)`.
- Optional with a default: `def greet(name, greeting = "Hello")`.
- Splat `*args` collects extra positional arguments into an array.
- **Keyword** arguments: `def connect(host:, port: 5432)`. `host:` is required, `port:` optional. Callers write `connect(host: "db", port: 6543)`, which is self-documenting and order-independent. Missing or unknown keywords raise `ArgumentError`.
- Double splat `**opts` collects extra keywords into a hash.
- A block parameter `&block` (covered with blocks).

Since Ruby 3.0, positional and keyword arguments are strictly separated: a hash passed positionally is no longer silently converted to keywords. Spread one explicitly with `**hash`.

Method names may end in `?` (predicates), `!` (dangerous or in-place) or `=` (setters). A method defined at the top level of a script becomes a private method on `Object`, callable anywhere in that script.

Methods can return multiple values as an array, which callers destructure: `min, max = bounds(list)`.
concepts.code:
def greet(name, greeting = "Hello", punct: "!")
  "#{greeting}, #{name}#{punct}"
end

def connect(host:, port: 5432, **opts)
  "#{host}:#{port} #{opts}"
end

def bounds(list) = [list.min, list.max]

puts greet("Ada")                       # Hello, Ada!
puts greet("Bo", "Hi", punct: "?")      # Hi, Bo?
puts connect(host: "db", ssl: true)     # db:5432 {ssl: true}

settings = { host: "cache", port: 6379 }
puts connect(**settings)                # cache:6379 {}

low, high = bounds([4, 9, 1])
puts "#{low}..#{high}"                  # 1..9

begin
  connect(port: 1)
rescue ArgumentError => e
  puts e.message                        # missing keyword: :host
end
takeaways: The last expression is the return value
Keyword arguments (name:) make calls self-documenting
Spread hashes into keywords explicitly with **
pitfalls: Passing a hash where keywords are expected without ** in Ruby 3, causing ArgumentError.

quiz.q: Given def f(a, b: 2), what does f(1, b: 5) return if the body is a + b?
quiz.explain: b: 5 overrides the default keyword, so 1 + 5 = 6.

concepts.name: Blocks and iterators
concepts.summary: Pass blocks to each, map and select, and write your own iterators with yield.
concepts.why: Blocks are Ruby's signature feature: almost every loop, callback and DSL in Ruby is a block.
concepts.body:
A **block** is a chunk of code passed to a method call, written with braces for one-liners or `do ... end` for multi-line code:

```ruby
[1, 2, 3].each { |n| puts n }
File.open("log.txt") do |f|
  puts f.readline
end
```

The method decides when and how often to run the block, passing values in through the `|params|`. Core iterators:

- `each` runs the block for each element and returns the receiver.
- `map` returns a new array of the block's results.
- `select`/`filter` keeps elements where the block is truthy; `reject` drops them.
- `find` returns the first match, `any?`/`all?`/`count` test conditions.
- `each_with_index`, `each_slice(2)`, `times`, `upto`.

Inside your own method, `yield` calls the block given by the caller, and `block_given?` checks whether there is one. Methods that set up and tear down something around a block (like `File.open`) are a key Ruby idiom: the cleanup happens even if the block raises.

Shorthands: `map(&:upcase)` calls a method on each element, and in Ruby 3.4 `it` refers to the single block parameter: `nums.map { it * 2 }`.

Blocks are closures: they can read and modify local variables from the surrounding scope. `next value` ends the current block call with that value; `break` exits the whole method call.
concepts.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
p nums.map { |n| n * n }          # [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]
p nums.select(&:even?)            # [2, 4]
p nums.find { it > 3 }            # 4 (Ruby 3.4 `it`)
p %w[a b].map(&:upcase)           # ["A", "B"]

def twice
  return :no_block unless block_given?
  yield 1
  yield 2
end
twice { |x| puts "got #{x}" }     # got 1 / got 2
p twice                           # :no_block

def timed(label)
  start = Time.now
  yield
ensure
  puts "#{label} took #{(Time.now - start).round(3)}s"
end
timed("sum") { (1..1_000_000).sum }   # sum took 0.0s (roughly)

total = 0
nums.each { |n| total += n }      # blocks see outer locals
p total                           # 15
takeaways: Blocks are code passed to methods; yield runs them
map transforms, select filters, each just iterates
&:method and it are shorthands for simple blocks
pitfalls: Using each when you need the transformed values; each returns the original array, not the block results.

quiz.q: What does [1, 2, 3].each { |n| n * 10 } return?
quiz.explain: each returns its receiver; use map to collect the block's results.

concepts.name: Classes and objects
concepts.summary: Define classes with initialize, instance variables and attr_accessor, and customise to_s and comparison.
concepts.why: Ruby is object-oriented to the core, and every gem and Rails app is built from classes.
concepts.body:
Define a class with `class Name ... end` and create instances with `Name.new(args)`, which calls `initialize`. **Instance variables** (`@name`) hold an object's state; they are always private to the object and spring into existence (as nil) on first use.

Expose state with accessor macros, which generate methods for you:

- `attr_reader :name` defines `name`.
- `attr_writer :name` defines `name=`.
- `attr_accessor :name` defines both.

Inside methods, call setters with `self.name = x`. Without `self.`, Ruby creates a local variable instead, a classic bug.

Visibility: methods are public by default; everything after `private` is callable only without an explicit receiver (from inside the object). `protected` allows calls from other instances of the same class.

Class methods are defined with `def self.create`, and class-level constants with `NAME = ...`. Inheritance uses `<`: `class Admin < User`, and `super` calls the parent's version of the current method (bare `super` forwards all arguments).

Useful hooks: define `to_s` for `puts` and string interpolation, `inspect` for `p`, and `==` for value equality. Include `Comparable` and define `<=>` to get `<`, `>`, `between?` and `clamp` for free.

For simple data holders, `Data.define(:x, :y)` (Ruby 3.2) creates an immutable value class with keyword or positional construction and value equality.
concepts.code:
class Account
  attr_reader :owner, :balance

  def initialize(owner, balance = 0)
    @owner = owner
    @balance = balance
  end

  def deposit(amount)
    raise ArgumentError, "amount must be positive" unless amount.positive?
    @balance += amount
    self
  end
  def to_s = "#{owner}: #{balance}"
end

acct = Account.new("Ada").deposit(50).deposit(25)
puts acct                # Ada: 75
p acct.respond_to?(:balance=)   # false: read-only

Point = Data.define(:x, :y)
a = Point.new(x: 1, y: 2)
p a                      # #<data Point x=1, y=2>
p a == Point.new(1, 2)   # true: value equality
p a.with(y: 5)           # #<data Point x=1, y=5>
takeaways: initialize sets up @instance_variables; Name.new calls it
attr_reader, attr_writer and attr_accessor generate accessors
Use self.attr = inside methods to call a setter
pitfalls: Writing balance = 10 inside a method meaning the setter; it creates a local variable. Use self.balance = 10.

quiz.q: Inside an instance method, what does name = "x" do when attr_accessor :name is defined?
quiz.explain: Bare assignment always creates a local variable; you need self.name = to call the setter.

concepts.name: Enumerable in depth
concepts.summary: Use Enumerable's power tools: reduce, group_by, partition, tally, each_with_object, sort_by and friends.
concepts.why: Idiomatic Ruby replaces most hand-written loops with one well-chosen Enumerable method.
concepts.body:
**Enumerable** is a module of 50+ methods available on any class that defines `each`, including Array, Hash, Range, Set and your own collections. Knowing the catalogue is what makes Ruby code short.

- Aggregation: `sum`, `count`, `min_by`, `max_by`, `minmax`, and `reduce(:+)` or `inject(0) { |acc, x| acc + x }` for anything custom.
- Grouping: `group_by { |w| w.length }` returns a hash of arrays; `partition` splits into two arrays (matches, non-matches); `tally` counts occurrences; `chunk_while` and `slice_when` split runs.
- Building: `each_with_object({}) { |x, h| ... }` passes the same accumulator to every call, and `to_h { |x| [key, value] }` builds a hash directly.
- Transforming: `flat_map`, `filter_map` (map and drop nils/falses in one pass), `zip`, `each_slice(n)`, `each_cons(n)`, `uniq`.
- Ordering: `sort_by { |u| [u.last, u.first] }` sorts by several keys; `sort` uses `<=>`; `max(3)` returns the three largest.

Hashes enumerate `[key, value]` pairs, so blocks can take `|k, v|`. They also have hash-returning versions: `transform_values`, `transform_keys`, `filter_map`, `select`, `sum`, `to_h`.

When a method takes a block and you call it without one, many return an Enumerator, so you can chain: `each_with_index.map { |x, i| ... }` or `map.with_index(1)`.
takeaways: Any class with each can include Enumerable and get 50+ methods
group_by, partition, tally and each_with_object replace manual loops
Block-less calls return Enumerators, enabling map.with_index and chaining
pitfalls: Using inject with a mutable accumulator but forgetting to return it from the block; use each_with_object instead.

quiz.q: What does [1, 2, 3, 4].partition(&:even?) return?
quiz.explain: partition returns two arrays: elements where the block is truthy, then the rest.

quiz.q: Why does inject({}) { |h, x| h[x] = 1 } fail on the second element?
options: The block returns 1, which becomes the next accumulator
quiz.explain: inject passes the block's return value as the next accumulator; each_with_object avoids this.

concepts.name: Modules and mixins
concepts.summary: Use modules as namespaces and mixins with include, extend and prepend, and implement Comparable and Enumerable.
concepts.why: Mixins are how Ruby shares behaviour across classes; Enumerable and Comparable are the most-used examples.
concepts.body:
A **module** is a container of methods and constants that can't be instantiated. It has two jobs.

As a **namespace**, it groups related classes: `module Billing; class Invoice; end; end` is referenced as `Billing::Invoice`. Gems put everything under one top-level module to avoid clashes.

As a **mixin**, it adds behaviour to classes:

- `include Mod` adds the module's methods as instance methods. The module is inserted into the class's ancestor chain just above the class.
- `extend Mod` adds them as methods on a single object, typically the class itself, so they become class methods.
- `prepend Mod` inserts the module *below* the class, so its methods run first and can call `super` to reach the class's own method. This is the clean way to wrap existing methods.

Mixins work through contracts. `Comparable` needs `<=>` and gives you `<`, `<=`, `==`, `>`, `between?` and `clamp`. `Enumerable` needs `each` and gives you `map`, `select`, `sort`, `sum` and the rest.

`Klass.ancestors` shows the lookup order, and `obj.is_a?(Mod)` is true for included modules. A module's `self.included(base)` hook runs when it is included, which is how libraries add class methods at the same time (Rails wraps this pattern in `ActiveSupport::Concern`).

`module_function` makes utility modules whose methods are called as `Mod.method`, like `Math.sqrt`.
concepts.code:
class Version
  include Comparable
  attr_reader :parts
  def initialize(s) = @parts = s.split(".").map(&:to_i)
  def <=>(other) = parts <=> other.parts
  def to_s = parts.join(".")
end

p Version.new("1.10.0") > Version.new("1.9.3")    # true
p [Version.new("2.0"), Version.new("1.2")].max.to_s  # "2.0"

class Playlist
  include Enumerable
  def initialize(*songs) = @songs = songs
  def each(&) = @songs.each(&)
end
p Playlist.new("b", "a", "c").sort               # ["a", "b", "c"]
module Loud
  def to_s = super.upcase + "!"
end
class Version
  prepend Loud
end
puts Version.new("3.4")                          # 3.4!
p Version.ancestors.first(3)                     # [Loud, Version, Comparable]
takeaways: Modules are namespaces and mixins; they can't be instantiated
include adds instance methods, extend adds singleton methods, prepend wraps
Comparable needs <=>; Enumerable needs each
pitfalls: Including a module expecting its methods as class methods; that's extend (or the included hook).

quiz.q: Which keyword lets a module's method run before the class's own method and call it via super?
quiz.explain: prepend places the module before the class in the ancestor chain.

quiz.q: What must a class define to get Enumerable's methods?
quiz.explain: Every Enumerable method is built on each.

concepts.name: Exceptions
concepts.summary: Raise and rescue exceptions, use ensure and retry, and design a custom error hierarchy.
concepts.why: Correct error handling separates scripts that silently corrupt data from programs you can trust.
concepts.body:
Signal an error with `raise ArgumentError, "bad id"` (or `raise CustomError.new(...)`). Handle it with `begin`/`rescue`/`else`/`ensure`/`end`:

- `rescue SomeError => e` handles that class and its subclasses; list several classes or several clauses, most specific first.
- `else` runs when no exception occurred.
- `ensure` always runs, which makes it the place for cleanup.
- `retry` inside `rescue` restarts the `begin` block; always cap attempts.

Method bodies and `do ... end` blocks act as an implicit `begin`, so you can put `rescue` and `ensure` directly in a `def`.

The hierarchy matters. A bare `rescue` catches **StandardError** and its subclasses: `ArgumentError`, `TypeError`, `NameError`, `NoMethodError`, `ZeroDivisionError`, `KeyError`, `IOError` and nearly everything an application raises. It deliberately does not catch `Exception` subclasses like `Interrupt` (Ctrl-C), `SystemExit` or `NoMemoryError`. Never write `rescue Exception` except at the very top of a process.

Define your own errors by subclassing `StandardError`, usually under one base class per library (`MyGem::Error`), so callers can rescue all of them at once. Wrapping a low-level error inside `rescue` automatically sets the new error's `cause`, preserving the original.

The inline modifier `value = Integer(s) rescue 0` exists but hides all StandardErrors; prefer explicit handling.
concepts.code:
class ShopError < StandardError; end
class OutOfStock < ShopError
  def initialize(item) = super("#{item} is out of stock")
end

def buy(item, stock)
  raise OutOfStock, item if stock.fetch(item).zero?
  stock[item] -= 1
end

stock = { tea: 1, cake: 0 }
%i[tea cake pie].each do |item|
  buy(item, stock)
  puts "bought #{item}"           # bought tea
rescue ShopError => e
  puts "shop: #{e.message}"       # shop: cake is out of stock
rescue KeyError
  puts "unknown item #{item}"     # unknown item pie
end
def with_log(name)
  yield
ensure
  puts "closed #{name}"           # runs even when the block raises
end
with_log("db") { Integer("42") }   # closed db
takeaways: rescue without a class catches StandardError, not Exception
ensure always runs; use it for cleanup
Give each library one Error base class subclassing StandardError
pitfalls: Writing rescue Exception, which also traps Ctrl-C and exit.

quiz.q: Which exception does a bare rescue NOT catch?
quiz.explain: Interrupt inherits from Exception (via SignalException), not StandardError.

concepts.name: Procs, lambdas and closures
concepts.summary: Turn blocks into objects with Proc and lambda, understand their differences, and pass methods around.
concepts.why: Callable objects power callbacks, strategies, Rails scopes and every DSL you'll meet.
concepts.body:
A block is not an object, but you can capture one. Declaring `&block` as the last parameter turns the caller's block into a **Proc** object you can store and call later with `block.call(x)` or `block.(x)`. The reverse, `&proc` at a call site, passes a Proc as a block.

Create callables directly:

- `square = ->(x) { x * x }` is a **lambda** (the `lambda { |x| }` form also works).
- `Proc.new { |x| ... }` or `proc { |x| ... }` creates a plain proc.

They differ in two ways:

- **Arity**: lambdas check the number of arguments like methods do; procs are lenient, filling missing args with nil and dropping extras.
- **return**: in a lambda, `return` exits the lambda. In a proc, `return` returns from the *method where the proc was defined*, and raises `LocalJumpError` if that method has already finished.

So lambdas behave like anonymous methods and are the usual choice for stored callables, such as Rails `scope :active, -> { where(active: true) }`.

All of them are **closures**: they keep access to the local variables in scope where they were created, even after that scope has returned. That's how counters and configuration callbacks work.

`obj.method(:name)` returns a `Method` object, and `&` converts it too: `%w[1 2].map(&method(:Integer))`. Callables compose with `>>` and `<<`, and `curry` creates partially applied versions.
concepts.code:
square = ->(x) { x * x }
inc = proc { |x| (x || 0) + 1 }

p square.(4)                  # 16
p inc.call                    # 1 (procs are lenient about args)
begin
  square.call
rescue ArgumentError => e
  puts e.message              # wrong number of arguments (given 0, expected 1)
end

def make_counter
  count = 0
  -> { count += 1 }           # closes over count
end
c = make_counter
c.call; c.call
p c.call                      # 3

def run(&block) = block.call(10)
p run { it / 2 }              # 5
p %w[1 2 3].map(&method(:Integer))   # [1, 2, 3]
pipeline = square >> inc >> :to_s.to_proc
p pipeline.call(3)            # "10"
p [square.lambda?, inc.lambda?]      # [true, false]
takeaways: &block captures a block as a Proc; &callable passes one as a block
Lambdas check arity and return locally; procs do neither
All are closures over the variables where they were created
pitfalls: Using return inside a proc that outlives its method, causing LocalJumpError.

quiz.q: A method defines pr = proc { return 1 }, calls pr.call, then has puts "after". What happens?
options: The proc returns 1 and the method continues
The method returns 1 immediately; after is not printed
quiz.explain: return in a proc returns from the enclosing method, so the rest of the method is skipped.

concepts.name: Pattern matching
concepts.summary: Destructure arrays and hashes with case/in, guards, pins and find patterns, and use => and in as one-liners.
concepts.why: Pattern matching makes handling JSON, API responses and nested data both concise and safe.
concepts.body:
`case`/`in` (stable since Ruby 3.0) matches a value against **patterns** that check structure and bind variables at the same time:

```ruby
case response
in { status: 200, body: { user: { name: String => name } } }
  greet(name)
in { status: 404 | 410 }
  not_found
in { status: Integer => code } if code >= 500
  retry_later(code)
end
```

Building blocks:

- **Value patterns** compare with `===`, so classes, ranges and regexes work: `Integer`, `1..5`, `/@/`.
- **Array patterns** `[x, y]` require exact length; `[first, *rest]` captures the tail; the find pattern `[*, { id: 3 } => hit, *]` searches anywhere.
- **Hash patterns** `{ name: }` match a subset of keys and bind `name`. Use `**rest` to capture the others or `**nil` to forbid extras. They match symbol keys only.
- `|` for alternatives, `=> var` to bind a sub-pattern, `if`/`unless` guards.
- `^var` **pins** an existing variable's value instead of rebinding it: `in { id: ^expected_id }`.

If no branch matches and there's no `else`, Ruby raises `NoMatchingPatternError`, which surfaces unexpected data early.

One-liners: `config => { db: { host: } }` destructures or raises, and `value in { type: :admin }` returns true or false. Classes opt in by defining `deconstruct` and `deconstruct_keys`; `Data` and `Struct` already do.
concepts.code:
def describe(event)
  case event
  in { type: "click", pos: [x, y] } if x.negative? || y.negative?
    "click outside"
  in { type: "click", pos: [x, y] }
    "click at #{x},#{y}"
  in { type: "key", key: "a".."z" => k }
    "letter #{k}"
  in { type: String => t, **rest }
    "other #{t} with #{rest.keys}"
  end
end

puts describe({ type: "click", pos: [3, 4] })   # click at 3,4
puts describe({ type: "click", pos: [-1, 0] })  # click outside
puts describe({ type: "key", key: "q" })        # letter q
puts describe({ type: "scroll", dy: 5 })        # other scroll with [:dy]

config = { db: { host: "localhost", port: 5432 } }
config => { db: { host:, port: } }
puts "#{host}:#{port}"                          # localhost:5432

expected = 2
found = ([{ id: 1 }, { id: 2 }] in [*, { id: ^expected }, *])
p found                                         # true
takeaways: case/in checks structure and binds variables in one step
Hash patterns match a subset of symbol keys; array patterns match exact length
Use ^ to pin an existing value; unmatched cases raise NoMatchingPatternError
pitfalls: Expecting in { x: } to match string-keyed hashes from JSON.parse; parse with symbolize_names: true.

quiz.q: Does { name: "Ann", age: 30 } match the pattern in { name: String }?
options: No, hash patterns need every key listed
Yes, hash patterns match a subset of keys
quiz.explain: Hash patterns ignore extra keys unless you add **nil.

concepts.name: Gems and Bundler
concepts.summary: Install libraries as gems, declare dependencies in a Gemfile, lock them with Bundler and run with bundle exec.
concepts.why: Every real Ruby project, Rails included, manages its dependencies with Bundler.
concepts.body:
A **gem** is a packaged Ruby library, published on rubygems.org. `gem install rubocop` installs one globally, and `require "json"` loads a library into your program. The standard library ships many default and bundled gems (json, csv, set, net-http, minitest).

For projects, use **Bundler**. A `Gemfile` declares what the project needs:

```ruby
source "https://rubygems.org"
gem "faraday", "~> 2.12"
group :development, :test do
  gem "rspec", "~> 3.13"
end
```

`bundle install` resolves compatible versions and writes `Gemfile.lock` with the exact version of every gem, including transitive ones. Commit the lock file for applications so every machine and server runs identical code. `bundle add faraday` edits the Gemfile and installs in one step; `bundle update faraday` deliberately upgrades one gem; `bundle outdated` lists available upgrades.

The pessimistic operator `~> 2.12` means `>= 2.12` and `< 3.0`; `~> 2.12.1` means `< 2.13`.

Run commands with **`bundle exec`** (`bundle exec rspec`) so they use the locked versions, not whatever is installed globally. In code, `require "bundler/setup"` does the same. Rails apps include binstubs like `bin/rails` that do it for you.

A library you publish is described by a `.gemspec`; `bundle gem name` scaffolds one. Version managers such as rbenv, chruby, asdf or mise switch Ruby versions per project via `.ruby-version`.
concepts.code:
# Shell session
bundle init                       # creates a Gemfile
bundle add faraday --version "~> 2.12"
bundle add rspec --group "development,test"
bundle install                    # writes Gemfile.lock

cat Gemfile.lock | grep -A1 "faraday ("   # exact resolved version

bundle exec ruby -e 'require "faraday"; puts Faraday::VERSION'
bundle outdated                   # what could be upgraded
bundle update faraday             # upgrade just this gem (within ~>)

echo "3.4.7" > .ruby-version      # picked up by rbenv / chruby / mise
bundle gem my_tool                # scaffold a publishable gem
takeaways: Gemfile declares dependencies; Gemfile.lock pins exact versions
Commit Gemfile.lock for applications
Use bundle exec (or binstubs) to run with the locked versions
pitfalls: Running a tool without bundle exec and getting a different global version than the project expects.

quiz.q: What range does gem "rack", "~> 3.1" allow?
quiz.explain: ~> with two segments allows the last one to grow, so >= 3.1 and < 4.0.

concepts.name: Files, IO and the standard library
concepts.summary: Read and write files safely with blocks, work with paths, and parse JSON and CSV from the standard library.
concepts.why: Scripting and data jobs, one of Ruby's strengths, are mostly reading, transforming and writing files.
concepts.body:
The simplest file operations are one-liners: `File.read(path)` returns the whole content, `File.write(path, text)` replaces it, and `File.readlines(path, chomp: true)` returns an array of lines. They are fine for small files.

For anything larger or longer-lived, use the **block form** of `File.open`, which closes the file even if an exception is raised:

```ruby
File.open("out.log", "a") { |f| f.puts "started" }
```

Modes: `"r"` read (default), `"w"` truncate and write, `"a"` append, `"r+"` read and write; add `"b"` for binary. `File.foreach(path) { |line| ... }` streams a file line by line in constant memory.

Paths: `File.join("data", "x.csv")`, `File.exist?`, `File.basename`, `File.extname`, `Dir.glob("logs/**/*.log")`, and `Pathname` for an object-oriented API. `__dir__` is the directory of the current file, useful for locating data next to a script.

Standard library helpers you will use constantly:

- `require "json"`: `JSON.parse(text, symbolize_names: true)` and `obj.to_json` or `JSON.pretty_generate(obj)`.
- `require "csv"`: `CSV.foreach(path, headers: true) { |row| row["email"] }`. Since Ruby 3.4 csv is a bundled gem, so add it to your Gemfile in Bundler projects.
- `require "fileutils"`: `mkdir_p`, `cp`, `rm_rf`.

Standard streams are `$stdin`, `$stdout` and `$stderr`; `warn "msg"` writes to stderr, and `ARGV` holds command-line arguments.
concepts.code:
require "json"
require "tmpdir"

Dir.mktmpdir do |dir|
  path = File.join(dir, "people.jsonl")
  File.open(path, "w") do |f|
    f.puts({ name: "Ada", langs: %w[ruby c] }.to_json)
    f.puts({ name: "Bo", langs: %w[go] }.to_json)
  end

  people = File.foreach(path).map { JSON.parse(it, symbolize_names: true) }
  p people.first                         # {name: "Ada", langs: ["ruby", "c"]}
  p people.sum { it[:langs].size }       # 3

  File.write(File.join(dir, "summary.json"), JSON.pretty_generate(people))
  p Dir.glob("#{dir}/*").map { File.basename(it) }.sort
  # ["people.jsonl", "summary.json"]
  p File.extname(path)                   # ".jsonl"
end
takeaways: Use File.open with a block so files are always closed
File.foreach streams large files line by line
JSON.parse(text, symbolize_names: true) gives symbol keys
pitfalls: Calling File.open without a block and forgetting to close the file.

quiz.q: Why prefer File.open(path) { |f| ... } over f = File.open(path)?
options: The file is closed automatically, even when an exception occurs
It reads the whole file at once
quiz.explain: The block form ensures close in an ensure clause when the block finishes.

concepts.name: Testing with Minitest and RSpec
concepts.summary: Write tests with Minitest's assertions and RSpec's describe/it/expect style, and stub collaborators.
concepts.why: Ruby's dynamic nature makes tests the main safety net, and the community treats them as non-negotiable.
concepts.body:
Ruby has two dominant test frameworks.

**Minitest** ships with Ruby (as a bundled gem) and is what Rails uses by default. Tests are classes inheriting from `Minitest::Test`, and every method starting with `test_` is a test:

- `assert_equal expected, actual`, `assert`, `refute`, `assert_nil`, `assert_includes`, `assert_in_delta` for floats.
- `assert_raises(KeyError) { ... }` returns the exception so you can check its message.
- `setup` and `teardown` run around each test.

Run a file with `ruby -Itest test/cart_test.rb`, or through Rake or Rails. Minitest also has a spec-style syntax (`describe`/`it`) and simple mocks and stubs (`Object#stub` from `minitest/mock`).

**RSpec** is the other big choice, with a descriptive DSL:

```ruby
RSpec.describe Cart do
  it "sums prices" do
    expect(Cart.new([2, 3]).total).to eq(5)
  end
end
```

It offers rich matchers (`eq`, `include`, `raise_error`, `change { }.by(1)`), `let` for lazily defined fixtures, `before` hooks, shared examples, and built-in doubles (`instance_double(Mailer, deliver: true)`), which verify that stubbed methods really exist.

Whichever you pick: test behaviour through public methods, keep each test independent, prefer dependency injection over global stubbing, and run the suite in random order (both do by default) to expose hidden coupling.
concepts.code:
# test_cart.rb: run with `ruby test_cart.rb`
require "minitest/autorun"

class Cart
  def initialize(prices) = @prices = prices
  def total = @prices.sum
  def item(i) = @prices.fetch(i)
end

class CartTest < Minitest::Test
  def setup
    @cart = Cart.new([2, 3.5])
  end

  def test_total
    assert_in_delta 5.5, @cart.total
  end

  def test_missing_item_raises
    err = assert_raises(IndexError) { @cart.item(9) }
    assert_match(/index 9/, err.message)
  end
end
# 2 runs, 4 assertions, 0 failures, 0 errors, 0 skips
takeaways: Minitest is built in: subclass Minitest::Test and write test_ methods
RSpec uses describe/it/expect with rich matchers and verified doubles
Tests run in random order, so keep them independent
pitfalls: Putting the actual value first in assert_equal, which makes failure messages misleading.

quiz.q: In Minitest, what is the argument order of assert_equal?
quiz.explain: assert_equal expected, actual; swapping them produces confusing failure messages.

concepts.name: The object model
concepts.summary: Understand singleton classes, method lookup through ancestors, self, and how class methods really work.
concepts.why: Every piece of Ruby metaprogramming, and much Rails magic, follows directly from the object model.
concepts.body:
In Ruby, classes are objects too: `User` is an instance of `Class`, which inherits from `Module`, which inherits from `Object`. Everything else follows from a few rules.

**Method lookup**: when you call `obj.foo`, Ruby looks in obj's **singleton class**, then its class, then each entry of `obj.class.ancestors` in order: prepended modules, the class, included modules (most recent first), the superclass, and so on up to `Object`, `Kernel` and `BasicObject`. The first match wins; `super` continues from there. If nothing is found, Ruby calls `method_missing`, which raises `NoMethodError` by default.

**Singleton classes**: every object can have its own hidden class holding methods for that object alone. `def obj.shout` or `obj.extend(Mod)` puts methods there. **Class methods** are simply singleton methods of the class object: `def self.create` inside `class User` defines `create` on User's singleton class. `class << self` opens that singleton class directly. Singleton classes of classes inherit from each other, which is why subclasses inherit class methods.

**self** changes with context: inside a class body it is the class, inside an instance method it is the instance. Calling a method without an explicit receiver sends it to `self`, and `private` methods can only be called that way.

Open classes let you reopen any class, even `String`, and add methods. This **monkey patching** is powerful and dangerous; prefer refinements or plain functions.
concepts.code:
module Greet
  def hi = "hi from Greet"
end

class Base
  def hi = "hi from Base"
end

class Child < Base
  include Greet
  def hi = "Child -> " + super
  def self.build = new        # singleton method of the Child object
end

p Child.ancestors.take(4)     # [Child, Greet, Base, Object]
puts Child.new.hi             # Child -> hi from Greet

obj = Child.build
def obj.hi = "only me"        # singleton method on one instance
puts obj.hi                   # only me
puts Child.new.hi             # Child -> hi from Greet
p obj.singleton_methods       # [:hi]

p Child.singleton_class.superclass   # #<Class:Base>
p Child.class, Class.superclass      # Class, Module
takeaways: Lookup goes singleton class, then ancestors in order; first match wins
Class methods are singleton methods on the class object
Calls without a receiver go to self; private methods require that
pitfalls: Monkey patching core classes globally, causing conflicts between gems.

quiz.q: Where does Ruby store a method defined with def self.find inside class User?
quiz.explain: def self.x defines a singleton method on the User class object, i.e. in its singleton class.

concepts.name: Metaprogramming
concepts.summary: Generate methods with define_method, call them dynamically with send, and handle unknown calls with method_missing.
concepts.why: Metaprogramming is behind attr_accessor, ActiveRecord attributes and most Ruby DSLs.
concepts.body:
Ruby lets code write code at runtime, and the core tools are ordinary methods.

- `public_send(:name, *args)` calls a method chosen at runtime. `send` does the same but also reaches private methods, so prefer `public_send`.
- `define_method(:name) { |args| ... }` creates a method from a block. Because the block is a closure, generated methods can capture loop variables, which is how `attr_accessor`-style macros are built.
- `instance_variable_get(:@x)` and `instance_variable_set` read and write state by name.
- `respond_to?(:name)` and `method_defined?` check for methods.

A **class macro** is just a class method called in the class body. When `has_flag :admin` runs, `self` is the class, so the macro can call `define_method` to add methods.

`method_missing(name, *args)` is called when lookup fails. It can implement dynamic finders or proxies, but always pair it with `respond_to_missing?`, call `super` for names you don't handle, and consider defining real methods on first use instead, which is faster and plays well with introspection.

Hooks let classes react to events: `inherited(subclass)`, `included(base)`, `method_added(name)`.

`instance_eval` and `class_eval` run a block with a different `self`; `class_eval` with a string compiles source code, which is fastest but needs care with untrusted input. Use these tools sparingly: metaprogrammed code is harder to grep, debug and type-check.
concepts.code:
class Model
  def self.flags(*names)
    names.each do |n|
      define_method("#{n}?") { @flags.include?(n) }
      define_method("#{n}!") { @flags << n; self }
    end
  end
  def initialize = @flags = []
end
class User < Model
  flags :admin, :verified
end
u = User.new.admin!
p [u.admin?, u.verified?]                 # [true, false]
p u.public_send(:verified?)               # false
class Settings
  def initialize(h) = @h = h
  def method_missing(name, *args)
    @h.key?(name) ? @h[name] : super
  end
  def respond_to_missing?(name, priv = false) = @h.key?(name) || super
end
s = Settings.new(theme: "dark")
p s.theme, s.respond_to?(:theme)          # "dark", true
begin; s.font; rescue NoMethodError; puts "no font"; end   # no font
takeaways: define_method plus closures generate methods from data
Prefer public_send to send so private methods stay private
Pair method_missing with respond_to_missing? and call super
pitfalls: Implementing method_missing without calling super, which silently swallows typos.

quiz.q: Why should method_missing call super for names it doesn't handle?
options: So unknown calls still raise NoMethodError instead of returning nil
quiz.explain: super reaches BasicObject#method_missing, which raises the normal NoMethodError.

concepts.name: Enumerators and lazy evaluation
concepts.summary: Build custom Enumerators, iterate externally with next, and process infinite or huge sequences lazily.
concepts.why: Lazy pipelines handle huge files and infinite sequences without building giant intermediate arrays.
concepts.body:
An **Enumerator** is an object that represents an iteration. You get one by calling an iterator without a block (`[1, 2].each`, `5.times`, `File.foreach(path)`), or build one from scratch:

```ruby
fib = Enumerator.new do |y|
  a, b = 0, 1
  loop { y << a; a, b = b, a + b }
end
```

Enumerators include Enumerable, so `fib.take(10)` works even though the sequence is infinite: the generator block only runs as far as needed. They also support **external iteration**: `e.next` returns the next value and raises `StopIteration` at the end, which `loop` rescues for you. `peek` looks ahead and `rewind` restarts.

Normally each Enumerable step builds a full intermediate array: `map` runs over everything, then `select` runs over the result. Calling **`lazy`** turns the chain into an `Enumerator::Lazy`, which pulls one element at a time through all the steps:

```ruby
(1..Float::INFINITY).lazy.map { it * 2 }.select { it % 3 == 0 }.first(3)
```

Nothing runs until a terminal method such as `first(n)`, `to_a`, `each` or `force` asks for values. Use lazy chains for infinite sources, huge files (`File.foreach(path).lazy`) and when you only need the first few results. For small in-memory arrays, the eager version is usually faster because laziness adds per-element overhead.

`Enumerator.produce(initial) { |prev| next_value }` (Ruby 2.7) is a concise way to generate sequences.
concepts.code:
fib = Enumerator.new do |y|
  a, b = 0, 1
  loop { y << a; a, b = b, a + b }
end
p fib.take(8)                       # [0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13]
p fib.lazy.select(&:even?).first(4) # [0, 2, 8, 34]

e = %w[a b].each
p e.next, e.next                    # "a", "b"
begin
  e.next
rescue StopIteration
  puts "done"                       # done
end

calls = 0
result = (1..Float::INFINITY).lazy
  .map { calls += 1; it * it }
  .reject(&:odd?)
  .first(3)
p result, calls                     # [4, 16, 36], 6

p Enumerator.produce(1) { it * 3 }.take(5)   # [1, 3, 9, 27, 81]
takeaways: Iterators called without a block return Enumerators
Enumerator.new and Enumerator.produce build custom, even infinite, sequences
lazy pulls elements through the chain one at a time until a terminal call
pitfalls: Calling a non-terminal like map on an infinite range without lazy, which never returns.

quiz.q: What does (1..Float::INFINITY).lazy.map { it * 2 } return?
options: An Enumerator::Lazy; nothing is computed yet
quiz.explain: Lazy chains build a description of the work; only a terminal method like first(n) runs it.

concepts.name: Building DSLs with blocks
concepts.summary: Combine blocks, instance_eval and method chaining to build readable internal DSLs like Rails routes and RSpec.
concepts.why: Much of the Ruby ecosystem (Rails routes, RSpec, Gemfiles, Rake) is a block-based DSL; knowing the trick demystifies them.
concepts.body:
An internal **DSL** is plain Ruby shaped to read like a configuration language. Rails routes, RSpec, Rake tasks, Gemfiles and Sinatra apps are all DSLs. They rely on three features you already know: optional parentheses, blocks, and changing `self`.

The key move is `instance_eval(&block)` (or `instance_exec(args, &block)`): it runs the caller's block with `self` set to a builder object, so bare method calls inside the block go to the builder:

```ruby
Router.draw do
  get "/users", to: "users#index"
end
```

Here `get` is a method on the builder, not on the code that wrote the block.

The trade-off is that inside the block, `self` is no longer the caller's object, so the caller's instance variables and methods disappear (local variables still work, since the block is a closure). For that reason many libraries offer a second form that yields the builder explicitly, `config do |c| c.port = 80 end`, which keeps `self` unchanged. Supporting both is easy: check `block.arity`.

Design tips:

- Keep the DSL small and make each method do one obvious thing.
- Store what the block declares and act on it later; don't do heavy work during evaluation.
- Validate eagerly and raise clear errors naming the DSL keyword.
- Use `Module#refine` (refinements, activated with `using`) rather than monkey patching if the DSL needs extra methods on core classes such as `5.minutes`.
concepts.code:
class RouteSet
  Route = Data.define(:verb, :path, :target)

  def self.draw(&block)
    set = new
    block.arity == 1 ? block.call(set) : set.instance_eval(&block)
    set.routes
  end
  attr_reader :routes
  def initialize = @routes = []
  %w[get post].each do |verb|
    define_method(verb) { |path, to:| @routes << Route.new(verb.upcase, path, to) }
  end
  def resources(name) = [get("/#{name}", to: "#{name}#index"), post("/#{name}", to: "#{name}#create")]
end

prefix = "/api"
routes = RouteSet.draw do
  get "#{prefix}/health", to: "health#show"   # locals still visible
  resources :users
end
routes.each { |r| puts "#{r.verb} #{r.path} -> #{r.target}" }
# GET /api/health -> health#show
# GET /users -> users#index
# POST /users -> users#create
takeaways: instance_eval runs a block with self set to a builder object
Inside such blocks, locals still work but the caller's methods and ivars don't
Offer a yield-the-builder form when callers need their own self
pitfalls: Referencing @ivars of the calling object inside an instance_eval block; they belong to the builder there.

quiz.q: Inside Router.draw { get "/x" } implemented with instance_eval, which object receives get?
options: The builder object that instance_eval runs on
quiz.explain: instance_eval changes self to the builder, so receiverless calls go to it.

concepts.name: Threads, the GVL and Ractors
concepts.summary: Use threads, Mutex and Queue for I/O concurrency, understand the GVL, and know what Ractors offer for parallelism.
concepts.why: Puma, Sidekiq and every concurrent Ruby service depend on how threads and the GVL behave.
concepts.body:
`Thread.new { ... }` starts a native OS thread; `join` waits and `value` returns the block's result. Threads share memory, so concurrent writes to shared state need synchronisation: `Mutex#synchronize`, or better, pass work through a thread-safe `Queue` (use `SizedQueue` for back-pressure).

CRuby has a **Global VM Lock (GVL)**: only one thread executes Ruby code at a time per Ractor. Consequences:

- Threads give real speedups for **I/O-bound** work. Blocking I/O, `sleep` and most C extensions doing I/O release the GVL, so ten threads can wait on ten HTTP requests at once. This is why Puma and Sidekiq use thread pools.
- **CPU-bound** Ruby code does not get faster with threads; use multiple processes (Puma workers, `fork`) or Ractors.
- The GVL is not a substitute for locking: `count += 1` is a read, an add and a write, and a thread switch can happen between them.

**Ractors** (experimental since 3.0) are actor-like units that run in parallel with separate GVLs. They can't share mutable objects: you send messages (copied or moved) and only shareable, deeply frozen objects cross freely. In 3.4 you exchange values with `send`/`receive` and get a result with `take`. Many gems are not Ractor-safe yet, so treat them as an option for isolated CPU work.

Other hazards: `Thread#raise` and `Timeout.timeout` interrupt code at arbitrary points, and an exception in a thread is only re-raised when you `join` it (set `Thread.report_on_exception`, on by default, to see it logged).
takeaways: The GVL lets only one thread run Ruby code at a time; I/O releases it
Threads speed up I/O-bound work, not CPU-bound Ruby
Protect shared state with Mutex or pass work through Queue
pitfalls: Assuming the GVL makes counter += 1 thread-safe; it can still lose updates.

quiz.q: A CPU-heavy pure-Ruby computation is split across 4 threads in CRuby. What speedup do you expect?
quiz.explain: The GVL serialises Ruby execution, so CPU-bound threads take turns; use processes or Ractors for parallelism.

quiz.q: Why do threads help a script that fetches 20 URLs?
options: Blocking I/O releases the GVL, so other threads run while one waits
The GVL is disabled for network code
quiz.explain: While a thread waits on the network it releases the GVL, letting the others proceed.

concepts.name: Fibers and the fiber scheduler
concepts.summary: Use Fibers as lightweight coroutines and understand how the fiber scheduler enables non-blocking I/O.
concepts.why: The Fiber scheduler lets Ruby run thousands of concurrent I/O operations with ordinary blocking-style code.
concepts.body:
A **Fiber** is a lightweight coroutine: it has its own stack, runs when you call `resume`, and pauses itself with `Fiber.yield`, handing a value back. Fibers are cooperatively scheduled, cost far less memory than threads and switch without OS involvement. External Enumerators (`e.next`) are implemented with fibers.

```ruby
f = Fiber.new { x = Fiber.yield(1); x * 10 }
f.resume      # => 1 (paused at yield)
f.resume(5)   # => 50 (yield returned 5; fiber finished)
```

Ruby 3.0 added the **fiber scheduler** interface. When a **non-blocking** fiber is running and a scheduler has been set with `Fiber.set_scheduler`, blocking operations like socket and pipe reads, `sleep`, DNS lookups, `Process.wait` and `Thread#join` call hooks on the scheduler instead of blocking the thread. The scheduler parks that fiber, runs others, and resumes it when its I/O is ready, typically using epoll, kqueue or io_uring.

Ruby ships only the interface; implementations come from gems, most notably **async** (with the Falcon web server). With it you write normal sequential code inside `Async do ... end` tasks and get event-loop concurrency without callbacks or `await` keywords.

Limits: it only helps I/O that goes through Ruby's IO layer or scheduler-aware C extensions. CPU-bound work, or a C extension that blocks without releasing control, still stalls every fiber on that thread. Fibers don't run in parallel; combine with processes for multiple cores.
concepts.code:
gen = Fiber.new do
  3.times { |i| Fiber.yield "step #{i}" }
  "finished"
end
4.times { puts gen.resume }      # step 0, step 1, step 2, finished
p gen.alive?                     # false

# Round-robin of cooperative tasks
tasks = %w[A B].map do |name|
  Fiber.new do
    2.times { |i| puts "#{name}#{i}"; Fiber.yield }
    :done
  end
end
until tasks.empty?
  tasks.reject! { |t| t.resume == :done }
end
# A0 B0 A1 B1 (one per line)

# With the async gem (Fiber scheduler), these 3 sleeps overlap:
#   require "async"
#   Async { 3.times.map { Async { sleep 1 } }.each(&:wait) }  # ~1s total
takeaways: Fibers are coroutines: resume runs, Fiber.yield pauses and returns a value
The fiber scheduler turns blocking I/O calls into event-loop switches
Ruby defines the interface; gems like async implement it
pitfalls: Expecting fibers to speed up CPU-bound work; they never run in parallel.

quiz.q: With a fiber scheduler set, what happens when a non-blocking fiber calls sleep(1)?
options: The fiber is moved to a new thread
The whole thread sleeps for 1 second
The scheduler parks the fiber and runs others until the timer fires
quiz.explain: Blocking operations are routed to scheduler hooks, which switch to other ready fibers.

concepts.name: Memory, GC and object shapes
concepts.summary: Learn how CRuby allocates objects, how its generational GC works, and how to find allocation hot spots and leaks.
concepts.why: Memory bloat and GC pauses are the most common performance problems in production Ruby services.
concepts.body:
CRuby stores objects in heap **slots**. Since Ruby 3.2, **variable width allocation** gives size pools (40, 80, 160, 320 and 640 bytes), so small strings and arrays live directly in the slot; bigger data is allocated with malloc. Immediate values (small Integers, Symbols, `nil`, `true`, `false`, most Floats on 64-bit) aren't heap objects at all.

The **garbage collector** is mark-and-sweep with two key optimisations:

- **Generational**: most objects die young, so frequent minor GCs scan only young objects, and objects surviving a few collections are promoted to the old generation, scanned only in major GCs. Write barriers track old-to-young references.
- **Incremental** marking splits major GCs into steps to shorten pauses. `GC.compact` (or `GC.auto_compact = true`) moves objects to reduce fragmentation.

Tools: `GC.stat` (counts of minor and major GCs, heap pages), `ObjectSpace.count_objects`, `ObjectSpace.memsize_of`, and the `memory_profiler` and `derailed_benchmarks` gems to find which lines allocate the most.

Allocation is the cost you control. Freeze string literals, avoid building throwaway arrays in hot loops (`each` instead of `map` when you ignore the result, `sum` instead of `map.sum`), and use `<<` rather than `+=` for strings. **Object shapes** (3.2) cache instance-variable layout per class; setting ivars in a consistent order, ideally all in `initialize`, keeps lookups fast for the interpreter and YJIT.

In multi-threaded servers, glibc malloc arena fragmentation can bloat memory; jemalloc or `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2` is a common fix.
concepts.code:
# frozen_string_literal: true
def allocations
  GC.disable
  before = GC.stat(:total_allocated_objects)
  yield
  GC.stat(:total_allocated_objects) - before
ensure
  GC.enable
end

nums = (1..1000).to_a
p allocations { nums.map { it * 2 }.sum }      # 3: includes a new 1000-element array
p allocations { nums.sum { it * 2 } }          # 1: no intermediate array

p allocations { s = +""; 100.times { s << "x" } }   # ~5: appends in place
p allocations { s = ""; 100.times { s += "x" } }    # ~100: new string each time

p 42.frozen?, :sym.frozen?             # true, true (immediates)
stat = GC.stat
p stat.slice(:minor_gc_count, :major_gc_count).keys   # [:minor_gc_count, :major_gc_count]
require "objspace"
p ObjectSpace.memsize_of("x" * 10_000) > 10_000       # true
takeaways: Small integers, symbols, nil and booleans are immediates, not heap objects
The generational GC makes short-lived objects cheap but not free
Measure allocations with GC.stat and memory_profiler before optimising
pitfalls: Optimising by guesswork instead of measuring allocations in the real hot path.

quiz.q: Why is nums.sum { it * 2 } cheaper than nums.map { it * 2 }.sum?
options: It avoids allocating an intermediate array
quiz.explain: map allocates a new array of results; sum with a block accumulates directly.

quiz.q: What does a minor GC scan?
options: Mainly young objects (plus old objects recorded by write barriers)
Only objects allocated by C extensions
quiz.explain: Generational GC focuses minor collections on young objects, using remembered sets for old-to-young references.

concepts.name: YJIT and performance tuning
concepts.summary: Enable YJIT, benchmark correctly, profile with stackprof or vernier, and write code the JIT can optimise.
concepts.why: YJIT gives real-world Rails apps large speedups for free, and profiling tells you where the rest of the time goes.
concepts.body:
**YJIT** is CRuby's just-in-time compiler, written in Rust by Shopify and production-ready since Ruby 3.2. It compiles hot methods to machine code using **lazy basic block versioning**: it generates code for a block only when it runs, specialised for the types actually seen. Typical Rails apps see 15 to 30 percent lower latency.

Enable it with `ruby --yjit`, the env var `RUBY_YJIT_ENABLE=1`, or at runtime with `RubyVM::YJIT.enable` (3.3+). Rails 7.2+ turns it on automatically in a generated initializer when available. Check with `RubyVM::YJIT.enabled?`, and read `RubyVM::YJIT.runtime_stats` when running with `--yjit-stats`. It costs some extra memory for compiled code; `--yjit-mem-size` caps it.

Code that YJIT, and the interpreter, handle well is **monomorphic**: call sites that see the same classes and object shapes every time. Initialise all instance variables in `initialize`, avoid redefining methods at runtime, and keep hot paths free of `method_missing` and heavy `send`.

Measure before changing anything:

- `benchmark-ips` reports iterations per second with error bars and warms up first, which matters with a JIT.
- **Sampling profilers** such as `stackprof` and `vernier` (which also shows GVL and GC time) find the slow code in a real workload, and `rbspy` attaches to a running process.
- Often the real cost is in SQL queries, N+1 loads or allocations, not Ruby execution.

Keep Ruby updated: each release brings substantial YJIT and GC improvements.
concepts.code:
# Run with: ruby --yjit bench.rb   (and compare with plain `ruby bench.rb`)
require "benchmark"

def fib(n) = n < 2 ? n : fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

puts "YJIT enabled? #{!!(defined?(RubyVM::YJIT) && RubyVM::YJIT.enabled?)}"
fib(20)                                 # warm up so hot code gets compiled
t = Benchmark.realtime { fib(27) }
puts "fib(27): #{t.round(3)}s"
# Typical: interpreter ~0.20s, YJIT ~0.05s (varies by machine)

# For real comparisons use benchmark-ips:
#   require "benchmark/ips"
#   Benchmark.ips do |x|
#     x.report("map.sum") { arr.map { it * 2 }.sum }
#     x.report("sum")     { arr.sum { it * 2 } }
#     x.compare!
#   end
takeaways: Enable YJIT with --yjit, RUBY_YJIT_ENABLE=1 or RubyVM::YJIT.enable
Monomorphic call sites and stable object shapes JIT best
Profile with stackprof or vernier and benchmark with benchmark-ips
pitfalls: Benchmarking without warm-up, so JIT compilation time pollutes the measurement.

quiz.q: Why should benchmarks of YJIT-enabled code include a warm-up phase?
options: Code is compiled lazily on first runs, so early iterations measure compilation
quiz.explain: YJIT compiles hot code as it runs; measuring before it stabilises mixes compile time into results.
